title: Vec Methods Practice
story: You're 30 minutes into debugging and realize your Vec has 0 items when it should have 50. Before you waste more time, you need to know: is the Vec empty? How many items does it have? Can I peek at the top without removing it?
why: `.is_empty()`, `.len()`, push+pop+get — mastering all Vec inspection methods prevents wasted debugging time.
analogy: Vec methods are like the dashboard of a car. `.is_empty()` is the fuel gauge — is there anything left? `.len()` is the odometer — how many miles (items)? Push/pop are the gas and brake pedals — add and remove. Together they give you complete control.
try_it: Build a complete stack with `push`, `pop`, `peek`, and `is_empty` functions. Then build a queue using Vec (enqueue adds to the end, dequeue removes from the front — you'll need to rebuild the Vec for dequeue). Test both with a sequence of operations: push(1), push(2), pop(), push(3), pop(), pop(), pop(). Compare stack vs queue behavior.
tips: `.is_empty()` is cleaner than `if len() == 0` — it reads like English and won't be wrong
Use `.get(len() - 1)` to peek at the last element without removing it
Stack = push + pop from the end. Queue = push to end, remove from front (harder with Vec, use a different approach)
common_mistakes: Calling `.pop()` on an empty Vec without checking `.is_empty()` first — you'll get None and might not handle it
Using `.len()` as the last index — the last valid index is `.len() - 1`, not `.len()`
Building a queue by removing from index 0 — this is O(n) with Vec; for queues, consider a different pattern
